w: Britain's official archive holds documents reaching back more than 1,000 years, free and open to the public. Formed from four former bodies -- among them the Public Record Office and HM Stationery Office -- it has hosted the Find Case Law database of senior court judgments since 2022.
s: Free public archive of 1,000+ years of British records
_facts: Holds documents dating back over 1,000 years
Free and open to the public
Formed from four former bodies including the Public Record Office
Hosts the Find Case Law database since 2022

w: A working botanic garden since 1759, Kew holds one of the world's largest herbaria -- over 8.5 million preserved plant and fungal specimens -- plus a library of 750,000 volumes. Its 132 hectares include four Grade I and 36 Grade II listed structures, and its own dedicated police force, running since 1845.
s: A 1759 botanic garden with its own police force since 1845
_facts: Founded 1759; 132 hectares, a World Heritage Site
Herbarium holds over 8.5 million plant and fungal specimens
Four Grade I and 36 Grade II listed structures on site
Has its own Kew Constabulary, operating since 1845

w: This red-brick Dutch House dates to 1631, raised atop the undercroft of an even older building, and is the chief survivor of a once much larger royal complex. Royals occupied it from around 1728 to 1818, plus a final stay in 1844; run, without government funding, by Historic Royal Palaces.
s: The Dutch House: Kew's surviving fragment of a royal palace
_facts: Known as the Dutch House, dating to 1631
Royal occupation from around 1728 to 1818, plus a brief stay in 1844
Grade I listed, open to visitors
Run by the independent charity Historic Royal Palaces, no government funding

w: Opened in 1863 but not finished until 1899, this Grade I glasshouse shelters Kew's largest plants beneath wrought-iron ribs by Decimus Burton and Richard Turner. A GBP15m restoration in 2011 fixed drainpipes the Victorians hid inside the stone columns, where trapped water had rusted the iron within.
s: Grade I glasshouse for Kew's biggest plants
_facts: Construction began 1860, completed 1899
Grade I listed; designed by Decimus Burton and Richard Turner
Houses Kew's largest plants
GBP15m restoration launched in 2011, finished 2014-15

w: Built in 1772 on the orders of Queen Charlotte, this thatched cottage orne sits within Kew Gardens on the banks of the Thames -- a picturesque garden retreat rather than a real residence. Grade II* listed, it is now looked after by Historic Royal Palaces and opens to visitors alongside the nearby Kew Palace kitchens.
s: Queen Charlotte's 1772 thatched garden retreat at Kew
_facts: Built 1772, commissioned by Queen Charlotte
An 18th-century cottage orne within Kew Gardens
Grade II* listed
Maintained by Historic Royal Palaces, open to visitors

w: Dating from the 1570s, this Georgian country estate straddles the boroughs of Ealing and Hounslow and was remodelled by Robert Adam between 1761 and 1765. Grade I and II listed, its park Grade II*, the estate has been open to visitors since the National Trust took charge in 1991.
s: Robert Adam's 1760s remodel, straddling Ealing and Hounslow
_facts: Estate dates from the 1570s
Straddles the London boroughs of Ealing and Hounslow
Main house remodelled by Robert Adam, 1761-1765
National Trust has managed it since 1991

w: Richard Boyle, 3rd Earl of Burlington, completed this Neo-Palladian villa in 1729, its garden by William Kent among the earliest English landscape gardens. Statesman Charles James Fox died here in 1806, Prime Minister George Canning in 1827; by 1892 it had become the Chiswick Asylum, later a fire station.
s: Neo-Palladian villa where Fox and Canning both died
_facts: Completed 1729 by Richard Boyle, 3rd Earl of Burlington
Garden by William Kent, an early English landscape garden
Charles James Fox died here in 1806; PM George Canning in 1827
Used as an asylum from 1892, later a fire station

w: Bought for the nation from the Rothschild family, this Grade II listed park opened to the public in 1926, unveiled by future PM Neville Chamberlain. Leopold de Rothschild's 19th-century woodland garden survives largely intact -- an Italian garden, a rock garden, an orangery, and an early Japanese garden.
s: Rothschild woodland gardens, opened to the public in 1926
_facts: Opened to the public in 1926 by Neville Chamberlain
Formerly the Rothschild family's estate
Grade II listed park and garden
Includes an Italian garden, rock garden, orangery and an early English Japanese garden

w: This Jacobean manor house was built in 1622 on the site of one of Middlesex's earliest medieval manors, its interiors altered over later centuries. Since 1965 its slice of the parish of Hanwell has belonged to Hounslow, and the adjoining public park keeps the lake that once served the house.
s: 1622 Jacobean manor house with a lakeside public park
_facts: Built 1622, Jacobean manor house
Sits on the site of an early medieval Middlesex manor
Since 1965 part of the London Borough of Hounslow
Boston Manor Park, with a lake, is the adjoining public green space

w: Dating from the 18th century -- the pub claims roots to 1650 -- this Grade II listed house on Burlington Lane was originally just The George, likely named for England's patron saint. Renamed by 1826 for the Duke of Devonshire, it is said to hide a smugglers' passage and pours beer from the neighbouring Griffin Brewery.
s: Old Chiswick riverside pub with a smugglers' cellar legend
_facts: Grade II listed pub on Burlington Lane, Chiswick
Claims roots back to 1650; renamed for the Duke of Devonshire by 1826
Legend of a smugglers' passage to riverside cottages
Serves beer from the neighbouring Griffin (Fuller's) Brewery
